summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Guinea-Bissau. The penal code decree of 1993 (Decree 4/93) contains no same-sex offences, and the country has never criminalised them. Guinea-Bissau signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity. Article 5 of the Law on Prevention, Protection and Combating Domestic Violence (Law 6/2014) provides that all victims, regardless of sexual orientation, hold the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity and are guaranteed equal opportunities to a life free from violence and to physical and mental health.

No legal gender recognition exists and no trans framework of any kind is on the record. There is no partnership or marriage recognition for same-sex couples, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, services or public life. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in access to health care, employment or education, while noting that anti-discrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals. Nothing in the sourced record documents an identity-document amendment route or a border-screening pathway for trans travellers, and none can be assumed.

The dominant visitor risk is state capacity and enforcement rather than any specific statute. The US State Department's 2012 report documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity; its 2011 report documents torture by security forces and impunity alongside female genital mutilation. The same 2012 report found that social taboos sometimes restricted freedom to express sexual orientation, and recorded societal stigma against LGBT people in the 2011 reporting. A travel-safety guide scores the country 34 out of 100, in its 'Caution' band, and reports no visible LGBT scene.

Reported violence is contested. The 2012 US State Department report recorded no reported violent incidents or human rights abuses targeting people on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, whereas a local NGO director stated in 2018 that there were some cases of violence targeting people on that basis and that Guinea-Bissau lacks legal protections for LGBTI people. Isolated violence cases are dated 2018.
tangentialFactors:
Public attitudes are comparatively moderate for the subregion but not permissive. A 2010 Pew Research Center study of nineteen African countries placed Guinea-Bissau among the most tolerant surveyed, with nine percent saying homosexual behaviour was morally acceptable and fifteen percent saying it was not an issue; a travel-safety guide repeats the nine percent figure. The US State Department's 2012 report characterised society as relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct while still finding that social taboos could restrict open expression of sexual orientation.

The wider security environment shapes visitor exposure more than any LGBT-specific rule: the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and the impunity enjoyed by perpetrators are documented in the 2012 US State Department report, with security-force torture also recorded in the 2011 report. In that environment, an incident involving a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor would sit inside weak investigative and prosecutorial machinery rather than a dedicated hate-crime regime, and no hate-crime enhancement covering gender identity appears anywhere in the record.

Guinea-Bissau's position differs from neighbouring jurisdictions that retain colonial-era sodomy statutes; here the 1993 penal code simply omits same-sex conduct, which removes prosecution risk but also leaves no statutory hook on which protections have been built.
localsOnly:
Government housing allowances are restricted by marital status and sex. Guidelines for civil servants' housing allowances limit family-size government housing to heterosexual married couples; same-sex couples receive the single-person allotment. The US State Department's 2011 and 2012 reports both record this rule.

Article 5 of Law 6/2014, titled the principle of equality, guarantees all victims of domestic violence, regardless of sexual orientation, the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity, equal opportunities to a life free from violence, and physical and mental health. This is the only explicit statutory protection naming sexual orientation in the record.

Residents have no anti-discrimination claim available under statute: anti-discrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals, according to the 2012 US State Department report, and no separate equality or gender-identity law exists. There is no recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriages, and no route to change legal gender markers on civil documents.

Adoption rules do not address LGBTQ applicants. A French government website states that single and married people are eligible to adopt without indicating whether LGBTQ people are disqualified.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, document amendment for trans people, or identity screening at entry. The absence of a trans framework is documented; the practical treatment of a trans traveller's passport at Bissau airport or in police checks is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The record on violence is internally inconsistent and cannot be reconciled from the available material: the 2012 US State Department report found no reported violent incidents based on sexual orientation or gender identity, while a local NGO director asserted in 2018 that such cases exist. Neither claim is independently corroborated here.

Adoption eligibility for LGBTQ applicants is unresolved: the sources state the general eligibility rules but do not say whether LGBTQ people are disqualified, and youth placement status is therefore unclear.

No youth-specific or minor-specific health access findings, and no findings specific to trans or LGBTQ minors, school students or youth travellers, appear in the sources. Health-care access for adults is covered only by the 2012 finding of no official discrimination, which does not describe the availability or quality of trans-specific care.
